segments.text: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events through which a plant cell grows, replicates its genetic material, and divides into two daughter cells — a fundamentally regulated process underlying the growth processes discussed throughout this subject, from meristematic growth (Topic 19) to embryo development (Topic 27) and, when regulation fails, potentially contributing to abnormal growth.
Phases of the cell cycle.
The cell cycle is broadly divided into
interphase
(the period between cell divisions, during which the majority of a cell’s total cycle time is typically spent, and during which the cell grows and prepares for division) and
M phase
(mitosis and cytokinesis, the actual division process). Interphase is further subdivided into:
G1 phase

(initial cell growth following the previous division, during which the cell carries out its normal metabolic functions and grows in size, and during which a key regulatory checkpoint determines whether the cell will proceed to DNA replication or, alternatively, exit the active cycle into a non-dividing resting state);
S phase

(DNA synthesis, during which the cell’s entire genetic material, its chromosomal DNA, is precisely replicated, connecting directly to the DNA replication mechanism discussed in Topic 81, producing two identical copies of each chromosome); and
G2 phase

(a further growth and preparation period following DNA replication, during which the cell continues growing and produces the proteins and cellular components necessary for successful division, along with a further regulatory checkpoint verifying that DNA replication has been completed correctly before the cell is permitted to proceed to mitosis).
Mitosis.

Mitosis is the process by which the replicated chromosomes are precisely separated and distributed into two genetically identical daughter nuclei, proceeding through recognised sub-stages (prophase, in which replicated chromosomes condense and become visible; metaphase, in which chromosomes align at the cell’s centre; anaphase, in which sister chromatids — the two identical copies of each replicated chromosome — are pulled apart toward opposite ends of the cell; and telophase, in which two new, separate nuclear envelopes reform around each set of separated chromosomes) — ensuring each resulting daughter cell receives a complete, identical copy of the parent cell’s genetic material.
Cytokinesis — a distinctively plant-specific process.

Following mitosis, cytokinesis physically divides the cell into two separate daughter cells; in plant cells specifically, this process differs notably from typical animal cell division, since the rigid cellulose cell wall (Topic 63) prevents the simple physical pinching-in mechanism animal cells use — instead, plant cells construct an entirely new cell wall structure (the cell plate) starting from the cell’s centre and progressively expanding outward until it fuses with the existing parent cell wall, effectively partitioning the original cell into two separate, independently walled daughter cells.
Cell cycle regulation and its significance.

The cell cycle is tightly regulated by specific checkpoint mechanisms (particularly at the G1 and G2 phase transitions noted above) that verify conditions are appropriate before allowing the cycle to proceed to the next stage — this regulation is essential to normal, controlled plant growth and development (connecting directly to the meristematic growth discussed in Topic 19 and to the coordinated cell division underlying tissue and organ development throughout this subject), and disruption of normal cell cycle regulation, whether through genetic mutation (Topic 73) or other causes, can result in abnormal, uncontrolled cell proliferation.
Key Takeaways

items.text: The cell cycle comprises interphase (G1 growth, S phase DNA replication, G2 further growth/preparation) and M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis), with regulatory checkpoints verifying conditions before each major transition.
Mitosis precisely separates replicated chromosomes into two genetically identical daughter nuclei through prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

Plant cytokinesis distinctively involves constructing a new cell plate from the cell centre outward (rather than pinching in, as in animal cells), reflecting the constraint imposed by the rigid plant cell wall.

segments.text: The plant cell wall and cell membrane together define the cell’s boundary and represent two structurally and functionally distinct layers — the cell membrane, shared in basic structure with all living cells, and the cell wall, a distinctively plant (and fungal, though chemically different, as established in Topic 5) structural feature providing essential rigidity and support absent in animal cells.
The cell membrane.

Composed primarily of a phospholipid bilayer (two layers of phospholipid molecules, each with a water-attracting “head” and water-repelling “tail,” spontaneously arranging into a stable bilayer structure with the water-repelling tails facing inward, away from the surrounding water-based environment) embedded with various proteins performing diverse functions — including the active and passive transport proteins discussed in relation to root water and mineral uptake (Topics 37 and 39), signalling receptor proteins (relevant to hormone reception, Topic 40, and cell communication, Topic 64), and enzymes. The cell membrane’s selective permeability (allowing some substances to cross relatively freely while restricting others, requiring specific transport proteins) is fundamental to the water potential and mineral nutrient uptake concepts discussed in Topics 36–39.
The cell wall.

Located external to the cell membrane, the plant cell wall is composed primarily of cellulose (a structural polysaccharide made of long chains of glucose molecules, distinct from the chitin composing fungal cell walls, Topic 5), organised into microfibrils embedded within a matrix of other polysaccharides (including hemicellulose and pectin) and, in some cell types, additional structural compounds such as lignin (a rigid compound providing substantial additional structural strength, particularly abundant in wood/secondary xylem tissue, connecting directly to the secondary growth discussion in Topic 20, and responsible for wood’s characteristic structural rigidity).
Functions of the cell wall.

These include providing structural support (both at the individual cell level and, cumulatively, at the whole-plant level, particularly significant in non-woody herbaceous plants, as discussed in relation to stem anatomy in Topic 22, where turgor pressure against a rigid cell wall provides much of the plant’s structural rigidity); defining and constraining cell shape and size (preventing the potentially damaging over-expansion that could otherwise occur when a plant cell absorbs water and increases in internal turgor pressure, Topic 36); and providing a degree of protection against pathogens (representing a physical barrier a pathogen must penetrate or otherwise overcome to successfully infect plant tissue, connecting to the plant disease process discussed in Topic 7) and against some forms of mechanical damage.
The middle lamella and plasmodesmata.

Adjacent plant cells are connected by a shared, pectin-rich layer called the middle lamella (essentially “gluing” adjacent cell walls together, explaining the coordinated, connected structure of plant tissue), while the plasmodesmata (microscopic channels through the cell wall connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, introduced in relation to the symplast water transport pathway in Topic 37) allow direct cell-to-cell communication and material transport without requiring substances to cross the cell wall and membrane barrier at each cell boundary — directly relevant to the cell communication mechanisms discussed further in Topic 64.
Key Takeaways

items.text: The cell membrane (a phospholipid bilayer with embedded transport, signalling, and enzymatic proteins) provides selective permeability fundamental to water and nutrient uptake; the cell wall (primarily cellulose, plus lignin in woody tissue) provides structural support external to the membrane.
The cell wall provides structural support, constrains cell shape against turgor pressure, and offers a physical barrier against pathogens and mechanical damage.

Adjacent cell walls are connected by the middle lamella, while plasmodesmata channels allow direct cytoplasmic connection and communication between adjacent cells, bypassing the wall/membrane barrier.

segments.text: Cell communication addresses the mechanisms by which plant cells coordinate their activities with one another — essential for the integrated, whole-organism-level responses discussed throughout this subject, including hormone signalling (Topic 40), stomatal regulation (Topic 23), and coordinated developmental processes (Topics 19, 62).
Major cell communication mechanisms in plants:

items.text: Direct cell-to-cell communication via plasmodesmata

— as introduced in Topic 63, plasmodesmata provide direct cytoplasmic connections between adjacent plant cells, allowing small signalling molecules, and in some cases even larger molecules including certain proteins and RNA molecules, to pass directly from cell to cell without crossing the cell membrane barrier — representing a distinctively plant mechanism for rapid, direct local cell-to-cell communication, functionally somewhat analogous to (though structurally quite distinct from) the gap junction communication mechanism found in some animal cell types.
Hormone signalling

— as discussed extensively in Topic 40, plant hormones represent a longer-distance communication mechanism, produced in one part of the plant and transported (through the vascular tissue or, in some cases, via more localised diffusion) to affect cellular behaviour in another part of the plant, binding to specific membrane-embedded or intracellular receptor proteins that trigger a specific cellular response cascade upon hormone binding.
Electrical signalling

— certain plants demonstrate rapid electrical signal transmission (action-potential-like signals, conceptually similar in basic underlying electrochemical principle to animal nervous system signalling, though generally propagating considerably more slowly and through different specific cellular mechanisms) enabling notably rapid response to certain stimuli — the well-known rapid leaf-closing response of the Venus flytrap and the touch-sensitive leaf-folding response of the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) represent particularly striking, visible examples of this electrical signalling mechanism in action, though electrical signalling is understood to play a broader, generally less visibly dramatic role in coordinating plant responses to various stimuli more generally, beyond these particularly well-known dramatic examples.
Chemical signalling between separate plants

— some plant species release volatile chemical compounds into the surrounding air in response to herbivore attack or other stress, which can be detected by and trigger defensive physiological responses in neighbouring plants (even genetically unrelated neighbouring individuals) before those neighbouring plants have themselves experienced direct attack, representing a form of inter-plant chemical communication of considerable ongoing scientific research interest, with potential practical relevance to crop protection strategies discussed in the Agriculture & Forestry subject.

segments.text: Why understanding cell communication matters.

Plant cell communication mechanisms collectively explain how a plant, despite lacking a centralised nervous system or brain comparable to animals, nonetheless achieves substantial coordinated, integrated physiological response across its entire body — from the localised cellular coordination underlying tissue development (Topic 19) to whole-plant-level responses to environmental stimuli including light (phototropism, connecting to auxin signalling, Topic 40), water stress (abscisic acid-mediated stomatal closure, Topics 23 and 40), and pathogen or herbivore attack.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Plant cell communication occurs through direct cytoplasmic connection via plasmodesmata, longer-distance hormone signalling, electrical signalling (dramatically visible in rapid-response plants like Venus flytrap and Mimosa pudica), and volatile chemical signalling between neighbouring plants.
These mechanisms collectively enable coordinated, integrated whole-plant physiological responses despite plants lacking a centralised nervous system comparable to animals.
Inter-plant chemical signalling in response to herbivore attack represents an area of active research interest with potential practical crop protection applications.

segments.text: Plant tissue and cell culture refers to the laboratory technique of growing plant cells, tissues, or organs in a controlled, sterile artificial environment, exploiting a fundamental property of plant cells — totipotency — with substantial practical applications extending throughout agriculture, horticulture, and plant genetic engineering.
The totipotency concept.

Plant tissue culture fundamentally relies on totipotency — the remarkable property, more pronounced and practically exploitable in plant cells than in most animal cells, by which a single differentiated plant cell retains the complete genetic information and developmental capacity necessary to regenerate into an entire, complete new plant under appropriate laboratory conditions, given the right combination of growth media and hormonal signals — directly connecting to the auxin/cytokinin balance discussed in Topic 40, since the relative concentration of these two hormone classes in the culture medium is a key factor determining whether cultured plant tissue develops predominantly roots, shoots, or an undifferentiated mass of dividing cells called callus.
Basic tissue culture process.

A small piece of plant tissue (an explant, potentially taken from various plant parts depending on the specific application) is surface-sterilised and placed onto a nutrient-rich, sterile culture medium (typically containing sugars, essential minerals connecting to Topic 39, vitamins, and a specific balance of plant hormones); under appropriate conditions, this explant tissue can be induced to proliferate (often first forming an undifferentiated callus mass, then subsequently, through appropriate hormonal manipulation, differentiating into organised root and shoot structures) and, ultimately, regenerate into a complete new plant, which can then be gradually acclimatised to normal soil and atmospheric growing conditions outside the sterile laboratory environment.
Practical applications:

items.text: Micropropagation

— rapid, large-scale clonal propagation of a desired plant genotype, particularly valuable for propagating plants that are difficult to propagate through conventional seed or cutting-based methods, or for rapidly multiplying a particularly valuable improved crop variety or elite genotype, connecting directly to the seed technology and genetic improvement discussions in the Agriculture & Forestry subject.
Production of disease-free planting material

— tissue culture, particularly using meristem tissue (Topic 19, since actively dividing meristematic tissue is often relatively free of systemic viral infection even in an otherwise infected parent plant), can be used to produce virus-free planting stock, of direct practical significance for vegetatively propagated crops (propagated from cuttings or tubers rather than seed) that would otherwise tend to accumulate viral infections across successive vegetative propagation generations.
Genetic engineering applications

— tissue culture techniques are frequently an essential component of the genetic engineering process discussed in Topic 84, since genetically modified individual plant cells must typically be regenerated into complete plants using tissue culture techniques before the introduced genetic modification can be expressed and evaluated in a fully developed plant.
Germplasm conservation

— tissue culture-based storage techniques can provide an alternative, space-efficient method for conserving plant genetic diversity, complementing conventional seed bank storage, particularly valuable for plant species whose seeds do not store well using conventional seed bank methods.

segments.text: Key Takeaways

items.text: Plant tissue culture exploits totipotency — individual plant cells’ retained capacity to regenerate into a complete new plant — using controlled combinations of nutrients and hormones (particularly the auxin/cytokinin balance) to direct tissue development.

Key applications include micropropagation (rapid clonal multiplication of valuable genotypes), producing disease/virus-free planting material, and serving as an essential step in genetic engineering (Topic 84).
Tissue culture also offers a space-efficient complement to conventional seed banks for conserving plant genetic diversity, particularly for species whose seeds do not store well conventionally.

segments.text: Cell senescence (the progressive decline in cellular function associated with aging) and programmed cell death represent normal, often genetically regulated processes within plant development and physiology, distinct from cell death resulting from acute injury or disease, and serving several important developmental and physiological functions.
Types of plant cell death.
Necrosis

refers to unregulated, typically damage-induced cell death (resulting from injury, extreme environmental stress, or pathogen attack, connecting to the plant disease processes discussed in Topics 7–9), generally an uncontrolled process that can trigger localised tissue damage extending somewhat beyond the initially affected cells.
Programmed cell death (PCD)

, by contrast, is a genetically regulated, controlled process in which specific cells are deliberately eliminated as part of normal plant development or in a specifically regulated defensive response — this controlled elimination process shares some underlying molecular mechanisms with the analogous, well-studied programmed cell death process in animal development, though the specific plant mechanisms show some distinctive features reflecting plants’ unique cell wall structure (Topic 63).
Developmental roles of programmed cell death.

These include xylem vessel formation (the mature, water-conducting xylem cells discussed throughout this subject’s water transport topics are, in fact, dead at functional maturity — during their development, these cells undergo a specifically regulated programmed cell death process that removes the cell’s internal contents while retaining the surrounding rigid, lignified cell wall structure, creating the effectively empty, hollow conducting tubes through which water moves via the cohesion-tension mechanism discussed in Topic 38); leaf and organ shedding (the process of leaf abscission, particularly pronounced in deciduous plants shedding leaves seasonally, involves a specifically regulated programmed cell death and cell separation process at the base of the leaf stalk, connecting to the hormonal regulation, particularly involving ethylene, discussed in Topic 40); and floral organ development (certain floral structures undergo programmed elimination of specific cells as part of normal flower development and maturation).
Defensive programmed cell death: the hypersensitive response.

A particularly significant defensive application of programmed cell death occurs in plant disease resistance: upon detecting pathogen attack (connecting to the plant pathology discussion in Topic 7), some resistant plants trigger a rapid, localised programmed cell death response at and immediately around the site of pathogen attack — this “hypersensitive response” effectively sacrifices a small number of the plant’s own cells at the infection site, but in doing so, deprives the invading pathogen (particularly pathogens requiring living host tissue to obtain nutrients) of the living tissue it needs to successfully establish and spread further, representing an effective localised defensive strategy that limits pathogen spread beyond the initial infection site at the cost of some localised tissue damage.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Necrosis represents unregulated, damage-induced cell death, while programmed cell death (PCD) is a genetically regulated, controlled elimination process serving specific developmental and defensive functions.
Developmental PCD roles include xylem vessel formation (mature xylem cells are dead, creating hollow conducting tubes), leaf abscission (seasonal leaf shedding), and floral organ development.

The hypersensitive response — a rapid, localised PCD triggered upon pathogen detection — sacrifices cells at the infection site to deprive the pathogen of living tissue needed to spread, representing an effective defensive strategy.

segments.text: Cellular ultrastructure examines the detailed internal organisation of plant cell organelles — the specialised, membrane-bound (in most cases) internal structures performing specific cellular functions — providing the microscopic structural foundation underlying many of the physiological processes discussed throughout this subject.
The chloroplast

, already discussed functionally in relation to photosynthesis (Topics 45–47), possesses a distinctive internal structure directly related to its function: enclosed by a double membrane (an outer and inner membrane, generally understood, along with certain other organelle features, to reflect chloroplasts’ evolutionary origin from a formerly free-living photosynthetic bacterium engulfed by an ancestral cell — the endosymbiotic theory, discussed further in relation to the origin of life in Topic 76), and containing an internal membrane system, the thylakoids (organised into stacked structures called grana in most plants), where the light reactions’ photosynthetic pigments and electron transport machinery are specifically located (Topic 45), surrounded by the stroma (the fluid-filled space where the carbon fixation reactions, Topic 46, occur) — chloroplasts also contain their own small quantity of DNA and can self-replicate somewhat independently within the cell, further evidence supporting their endosymbiotic evolutionary origin.
The mitochondrion

, discussed functionally in relation to respiration (Topics 48–50), similarly possesses a double membrane structure (also reflecting endosymbiotic origin, in this case from an ancestral free-living bacterium capable of aerobic respiration) — with the inner membrane characteristically folded into extensive invaginations called cristae, substantially increasing the inner membrane’s total surface area available to house the electron transport chain and ATP synthase enzyme complexes central to oxidative phosphorylation (Topic 50), directly connecting this structural feature to the mitochondrion’s central respiratory function; the fluid-filled interior space (the matrix) houses the Krebs cycle enzymes (Topic 49).
The nucleus

, containing the cell’s genetic material (chromosomal DNA, discussed in relation to the cell cycle in Topic 62 and DNA structure in Topic 79), is enclosed by a double membrane nuclear envelope, perforated by nuclear pores that regulate the selective passage of molecules (including RNA molecules produced through the transcription process discussed in Topic 82) between the nucleus and the surrounding cytoplasm.
The vacuole — a particularly prominent and functionally distinctive plant cell organelle.

Mature plant cells characteristically contain a large, often single central vacuole, frequently occupying the substantial majority of the total cell volume — considerably more prominent than the generally smaller, more numerous vacuoles found in most animal cells — serving several important functions: maintaining turgor pressure (Topic 36, since the vacuole’s fluid content, and the resulting pressure exerted against the surrounding cell wall, is the primary contributor to overall cell turgor); storage (of water, dissolved nutrients, and various metabolic products, including, in some plant tissues, stored sugars or pigment compounds); and, in some cases, storage of potentially harmful metabolic waste products or defensive secondary metabolite compounds (Topic 33) safely sequestered away from other more sensitive cellular components.
The endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and ribosomes

perform protein and other biomolecule synthesis, processing, and transport functions broadly analogous to their well-characterised roles in other eukaryotic cells generally, supporting the cell’s overall biosynthetic and secretory processes, including the synthesis of cell wall materials (Topic 63) and various proteins essential to the diverse cellular processes discussed throughout this subject.
Key Takeaways

items.text: The chloroplast (photosynthesis) and mitochondrion (respiration) both possess double membranes reflecting their endosymbiotic evolutionary origin from formerly free-living bacteria, with internal structures (thylakoid/grana; cristae) directly reflecting and maximising their respective functional processes.
The nucleus houses chromosomal DNA within a pore-perforated double membrane envelope regulating molecular exchange with the cytoplasm.
The large central vacuole, a particularly prominent and distinctive plant cell feature, maintains turgor pressure and provides storage for nutrients, metabolic products, and defensive compounds.
